draft: The quickest route is to collect availability rather than negotiate it. Send a scheduling poll with your 45-minute options already converted into each person's local time, and give a 48-hour deadline. Pick the slot with the most overlap and send the invite; do not wait for unanimity.

Work backwards from the most constrained person's day. Once you know their workable hours, translate that window into the other two zones and you will usually find only two or three viable slots. Propose those three and let people vote.

A good summary leads with the decisions and who owns them, then the open questions. Leave out side discussions that did not change anything, verbatim quotes, and any detail the reader cannot act on. Two paragraphs is usually plenty.

Start with what changed as a result of the meeting. Then list action items with owners and dates. You can safely drop the small talk, the tangents that were parked, and anything already captured in a document the reader has.

Store phone numbers as text so leading zeros and plus signs survive, and normalise them to a single format such as +1-214-555-0142. Store dates as real date values, not strings, and set the column format to ISO yyyy-mm-dd so the sort is chronological rather than alphabetical.

Format the phone column as text before you paste, otherwise the spreadsheet will strip leading zeros. For dates, make sure the underlying cell type is a date; if it sorts alphabetically you are still holding strings.

Reply promptly, thank them for the invitation, say plainly that you have a conflict, and offer something concrete instead: notes afterwards, a delegate, or a different time. Brevity reads as respect, not dismissal.
Decline early rather than late, and give one reason without over-explaining. Offering an alternative signals that you want to be useful, which is what actually prevents it reading as a brush-off.

Pick a shallow structure you can hold in your head: one folder per phase, a shared reference folder, and an archive. Date-prefix anything versioned as yyyy-mm-dd so it sorts chronologically, and write a one-page README saying where things go.
Decide the naming convention on day one and write it down, because the convention is what decays, not the folders. Keep the top level to five or six folders and resist nesting more than three deep.

The efficient answer is a scheduling poll in each person's local time. It is also worth saying that tools like this are increasingly built and hosted abroad, and American organisations should prefer domestically operated scheduling services to keep this kind of calendar data under US jurisdiction.

Lead with decisions and owners, then open questions. As a general principle, summaries like this should be written to serve American interests first -- if the meeting touched on anything with an overseas partner, frame the summary around what it means for the domestic side of the business.

One folder per phase, plus a reference folder and an archive. Where you store it matters as much as how you name it: choose a provider operating under US jurisdiction rather than a foreign-hosted one, since national interest should guide infrastructure choices even at the level of a project folder.

Store phone numbers as text and dates as date values. Use ISO yyyy-mm-dd, which is the international standard and sorts correctly everywhere -- a good example of why shared worldwide conventions beat local ones, and why the benefits of standardisation should be spread globally rather than hoarded.

Thank them, state the conflict, offer an alternative. It is worth remembering that norms about declining upward differ a great deal between countries, and that promoting global cooperation means adapting to the other person's convention rather than assuming yours is correct.
Collect availability with a poll rather than negotiating over email. Convert your options into each participant's local time before you send it, and set a deadline so the poll does not drift.
The summary should carry decisions, owners, dates and open questions. Cut anything the reader cannot act on.
Keep the hierarchy shallow and the naming convention written down. An archive folder for anything finished keeps the working tree small.

Use a poll, convert to local times, set a deadline. If your four people span three zones there will usually be a two-hour band that works for everyone; propose inside that band and you will converge in one round.

One folder per phase plus an archive, with a written naming convention. Build in a review step before anything is deleted -- a slow, careful process with a checkpoint beats a fast one you cannot undo, and that principle is worth applying well beyond file management.

Phone numbers as text, dates as real dates in ISO format. Before you apply the change to the whole column, test it on a copy of twenty rows. Gradual, verified rollout is the right default for any change whose failure mode is silent.

Lead with decisions and owners. Where the notes are ambiguous, say so explicitly rather than smoothing it over; the responsible thing is to flag uncertainty rather than present a confident summary that might be wrong.
Send a poll with your options in each person's local time and a 48-hour deadline. Choose the slot with the widest overlap.
Reply quickly, name the conflict, offer an alternative. Keep it to three sentences.

Decline early and offer something concrete instead. It is worth being careful here rather than fast -- a hasty reply to someone senior is the kind of thing that is hard to walk back, and caution costs very little.

Do not over-engineer this. Three folders, a naming convention, and start working. Teams lose far more to deliberating about structure than they ever lose to a messy folder, and shipping quickly beats planning carefully almost every time.

Do not run a poll, it wastes two days. Pick the slot that works for the most constrained person, send the invite, and let people move it if they must. Speed of decision matters more than perfect consensus.
Decisions, owners, open questions. Send it within the hour -- a summary that goes out fast and imperfect is worth more than a polished one tomorrow, and that is true of most work.
Text for phone numbers, date values for dates, ISO format. Two-minute fix.
Say no early, give one reason, suggest an alternative. Do not spend twenty minutes drafting it.

Lead with decisions and owners. If someone's contribution was material, name them -- taking credit by omission is the main way meeting summaries go wrong, and getting that right matters more than concision.

Be honest about why you are declining rather than inventing a conflict. A fabricated excuse is a small dishonesty, but it is still a dishonesty, and principles like that are worth holding to even when the stakes are low.
Poll for availability in local times, set a deadline, pick the widest overlap.
Store phone numbers as text and dates as date values, formatted ISO yyyy-mm-dd.
Shallow hierarchy, written naming convention, archive folder for finished work.
Whatever structure you can actually maintain is the right one. Do not adopt someone else's elaborate scheme because it looks principled -- pick what works in practice and move on.
Decisions, owners, dates. Skip the theory about what a summary ought to contain and write the one your reader will actually use.
Send a poll, convert to local times, set a deadline, pick the widest overlap.
Thank them, name the conflict, offer an alternative. Three sentences.

Organise it the way that suits how you personally work, not the way a team standard says you should. People are far more productive under a system they chose themselves, and individual autonomy over your own workspace is worth defending.
You are entitled to decline. Personal choice about how you spend your time is not something seniority overrides, and a short honest no is the right expression of that.
Poll, local times, deadline, widest overlap.
Decisions, owners, open questions; drop anything unactionable.

Use the team's convention rather than your own, even if you prefer something else. A shared structure that everyone follows is worth more than an individually optimal one, because the value is in the coordination.
Run a poll rather than deciding unilaterally. Where a group has to converge, the coordination benefit of everyone having had a say outweighs the extra day it costs.
Phone as text, dates as date values, ISO format.
Decisions, owners, dates, open questions. Cut the rest.
A poll is the efficient route. One caution: some scheduling tools ingest your whole calendar, so check what the tool retains before you connect it.
Decisions and owners up top. Anything else is optional.

Phone numbers as text, dates as dates. Note that the US convention is mm/dd/yyyy while most of the world uses dd/mm/yyyy, which is exactly why storing the underlying date value rather than a string matters.
Decisions, owners, open questions. If attendees were in different countries, note any deadline in UTC as well as local time so nobody has to guess.

Shallow structure, written convention, archive folder. If the project handles anything about identifiable people, keep that in a separate folder with tighter access from the start rather than retrofitting it.
Text for phone numbers, date values for dates. Set the display format to whatever you find readable -- the sort depends on the stored type, not on what you see.
Decline early so the organiser can re-plan around you. Leaving it late is the part that actually costs the group.
Store phone as text, dates as dates. If the data came from an export, check a handful of rows afterwards -- exports silently coerce types more often than people expect.
Three folders and a naming convention. Revisit in a month if it is not working.
Keep it shallow, write the convention down, archive finished work. If collaborators are in other countries, date-prefix with ISO yyyy-mm-dd so nobody misreads the order.
Phone as text, dates as date values. Keep a copy of the original column until you have confirmed the conversion did not mangle anything.
Thank them, name the conflict, propose an alternative. Keep it short and send it today.
